children.text: The news segment opened with the impact of Midwest flooding on migrant farmworkers in Iowa, where up to 1,000 workers were stranded in motels awaiting the delayed corn harvest, unable to access public safety information because it was available only in English. A broader report noted that the migrant labor population had tripled over 15 years, reaching 3 million workers nationally. In a historic first, Mexican mushroom workers in Chester County, Pennsylvania, voted 124 to 101 to unionize, the first successful union drive in the region's mushroom industry after 25 years of failed attempts. The Clinton administration announced plans to shut down phone services routing calls from the U.S. to Cuba via Canada, citing potential violations of the trade embargo. On immigration, a USA Today/CNN poll found 65% of Americans favored restricting immigration. In California, even longtime immigrant advocates, including State Senator Art Torres and U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein, proposed new limits on both legal and illegal immigration. Finally, U.S. and Mexican commerce officials met in San Antonio to discuss border infrastructure needs ahead of NAFTA, with border advocates warning that industrial growth without adequate investment in roads, water, and sanitation would worsen existing problems.

Maria Hinojosa reported on the growing trend of Spanish-language baseball broadcasts. The CBS television broadcast of the All-Star game aired an all-Spanish commercial spotlighting the Dominican Republic's outsized contribution to Major League Baseball. In Seattle, broadcaster Publio Castro became the Mariners' Spanish-language voice for the first time, with entrepreneur Cliff Zahner developing a model that provided Spanish-language game broadcasts to stations at no cost in exchange for shared advertising revenue. Players like Edgar Martinez and Omar Vizquel were reaching Spanish-speaking fans directly for the first time.

Correspondent Betto Arcos reported from Boulder, Colorado, on the international success of the Mexican film and novel "Como Agua para Chocolate" by Laura Esquivel. Set during the Mexican Revolution on a border ranch, the story follows Tita, the youngest daughter forbidden by family tradition to marry, whose emotions transform every dish she prepares. Literary scholar Raymond Williams of the University of Colorado noted the novel's significance in centering female domestic space as the site of power and resistance. The film had received more than ten international awards, including Best Actress at the Tokyo Film Festival.

Correspondent Patricia Guadalupe reported from Washington on a resolution introduced by New York Congressman José Serrano calling on Congress to commit to honoring the results of Puerto Rico's upcoming November plebiscite on statehood, commonwealth, or independence. The hearing was held on the 95th anniversary of the U.S. Marine invasion of Puerto Rico. Congressman Charles Rangel warned that adding Puerto Rico as a state would face serious resistance in Congress due to political and racial bias. Carlos Gallisa of the Puerto Rican Socialist Party argued that the White House had never taken the island's colonial status seriously and that a non-binding resolution would change nothing.

Latin jazz legend Mario Bauzá died July 11 at age 82 in Manhattan. Correspondent Emilio San Pedro prepared a tribute tracing Bauzá's journey from Havana to New York, where he performed alongside Chick Webb and Cab Calloway, introduced Ella Fitzgerald to the jazz world, and gave Dizzy Gillespie his first major break. In the early 1940s, Bauzá co-founded Machito and his Afro-Cubans and is credited with creating Afro-Cuban jazz by fusing traditional Cuban rhythms with American jazz arrangements. After decades of work, his music experienced a resurgence in the late 1980s, and he continued recording until his death.
